content: 1. Individuals at higher risk of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection include those from populations with elevated seroprevalence, such as mobile and migrant groups from regions with high or intermediate HBV endemicity, and certain indigenous populations. Additionally, those with a history of high-risk behaviors, such as people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or other closed settings, men who have sex with men, sex workers, people living with HIV, and close contacts (partners, family members, or children) of individuals with hepatitis B, are also at increased risk. 2. Clinical features that may suggest underlying chronic hepatitis B (CHB) include evidence of existing liver disease, such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), or unexplained liver abnormalities, including abnormal liver function tests or findings on liver ultrasound. 3. In all settings, it is recommended to perform hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) serological testing. For those who test HBsAg-negative and have not been previously vaccinated, hepatitis B vaccination should be offered. This is particularly important for children with parents or siblings diagnosed with HBV infection or those with clinical suspicion of hepatitis. Testing can be conducted through communityor facility-based programs. 4. For diagnosing CHB in individuals older than 12 months, a serological assay (either rapid diagnostic test [RDT] or laboratory-based immunoassay) that meets minimum quality, safety, and performance standards is recommended to detect HBsAg. Laboratory-based immunoassays are preferred in settings with accessible laboratory testing, while RDTs are recommended in areas with limited laboratory access to improve linkage to care and treatment. 5. A single HBsAg assay is recommended as an initial step before further evaluation for HBV DNA levels and liver disease staging. Chronic HBV infection is confirmed by the persistence of HBsAg for six months or more. 6. Infants exposed to HBV should be tested for HBsAg between 6 and 12 months of age to screen for evidence of infection. Testing within the first six months of life is challenging due to inconsistent detectability of HBsAg and HBV DNA in infected infants. 7. Acute HBV infection can be confirmed by the presence of HBsAg and IgM anti-HBc antibodies. CHB is diagnosed when HBsAg persists for six months or longer. 8. Laboratory-based immunoassays, such as enzyme immunoassay, chemiluminescence immunoassay, and electrochemiluminescence assay, should meet minimum acceptance criteria established by WHO or stringent regulatory reviews. These assays must be used according to manufacturers' instructions and, where possible, at testing sites enrolled in external quality assessment schemes. 9. Predictive modeling of seroprevalence and assay diagnostic performance informs testing strategies. In some cases, repeat HBsAg testing after six months is used to confirm chronicity. 10. Antiviral therapy should be initiated in individuals with CHB who meet specific criteria, such as persistently abnormal alanine aminotransferase (ALT) levels, HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL, or the presence of co-infections, comorbidities, immune suppression, family history of liver cancer or cirrhosis, or extrahepatic manifestations. Treatment options include tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), entecavir (ETV), or tenofovir alafenamide (TAF) in specific populations, such as those with osteoporosis or impaired kidney function. 11. Pregnant women with CHB should be reassessed after delivery, as ALT levels may normalize during pregnancy and are not reliable markers for long-term treatment decisions during this period. 12. All individuals with CHB should undergo regular monitoring for disease activity, progression, and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) detection. More frequent monitoring is required for those with advanced liver disease, during the first year of treatment, or if adherence is a concern. 13. Infants born to HBsAg-positive mothers should receive a timely birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine within 24 hours, followed by 2 or 3 additional doses, regardless of the mother's HBsAg status. 14. Maternal antiviral prophylaxis with tenofovir is recommended for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with high HBV DNA levels (≥200,000 IU/mL) or HBeAg positivity, starting from at least the second trimester until after delivery, to prevent mother-to-child transmission. 15. The updated guidelines aim to expand treatment eligibility, simplify diagnostic thresholds, and promote equitable access to care. They emphasize a public health approach to scaling up HBV testing and treatment, ensuring access to high-quality services while addressing stigma and discrimination. 16. The guidelines also advocate for person-centered care, simplified service delivery, and integration of hepatitis services with other health programs. Strategies include strengthening linkage to care, promoting adherence, decentralizing services, and engaging communities to improve access and retention in care. 17. Implementation of these recommendations should be adapted to local contexts, considering national HBV epidemiology, health system capacity, and available resources.
